learn.title: Lithium-Ion Batteries: Storing Solar and Wind Energy
learn.intro: Lithium-ion batteries are key to balancing renewable energy supply and demand. They store excess solar and wind power during peak production and release it when generation drops, ensuring reliable electricity even when the sun isn’t shining or wind isn’t blowing. This technology is transforming how we integrate renewables into the grid.
learn.c1_text: A lithium-ion battery cell works like a rechargeable sponge, soaking up lithium ions when charging and releasing them when discharging. Think of it like a water tank: energy flows in during surplus periods and flows out during shortages. These cells are arranged in modules, then packs, to power everything from phones to electric buses.
learn.c2_text: At grid scale, lithium-ion systems act like massive reservoirs of stored electricity. For example, Tesla’s Hornsdale Powerpack in Australia stores 150 MWh—enough to power 30,000 homes for an hour. These installations help stabilize frequency, defer transmission upgrades, and provide backup during outages, making renewables more dispatchable and dependable.
learn.c3_text: India is rapidly adopting battery storage to manage its growing renewable capacity. As of 2024, India has over 90 GW of solar and 45 GW of wind energy. The government aims to deploy 4-hour storage solutions alongside renewables to ensure grid stability and reduce curtailment of clean energy.

learn.title: Power Purchase Agreements: Financing Renewable Projects
learn.intro: Power Purchase Agreements (PPAs) are long-term contracts that enable renewable energy projects to secure financing and sell electricity at fixed rates. They bridge the gap between developers and buyers, reducing financial risk and accelerating clean energy deployment. PPAs are essential tools for corporate sustainability and grid expansion.
learn.c1_text: A Power Purchase Agreement is a contract where a buyer agrees to purchase electricity from a generator at a predetermined price over 10–25 years. Think of it like a lease-to-own model: the developer builds the plant, and the buyer commits to buying the power. This guarantees revenue, unlocking loans and investments needed to build the project.
learn.c2_text: Large corporations sign virtual PPAs to meet sustainability goals without taking physical delivery of electrons. For instance, Google signed a PPA for 1.6 GW of wind power in the U.S. The company receives renewable energy credits and pays the market difference if prices fluctuate. This helps scale up clean energy while hedging energy costs.
learn.c3_text: In India, utilities and large industries sign PPAs with solar and wind farms to meet Renewable Purchase Obligations. As of 2023, over 175 GW of renewable projects are operational or under development. PPAs help DISCOMs meet RPO targets and attract private investment into the sector.

learn.title: Wave Energy Converters: Harvesting Ocean Power
learn.intro: Wave energy converters capture the kinetic and potential energy of ocean waves to generate clean electricity. With oceans covering 70% of Earth’s surface, this vast and predictable resource could significantly contribute to global energy needs. Unlike solar and wind, wave energy is highly consistent and less weather-dependent.
learn.c1_text: There are several types of wave energy converters. Point absorbers float on the surface and move up and down with waves, driving hydraulic pistons. Oscillating water columns use wave motion to compress air and spin turbines—like a giant organ pipe powered by the sea. Each design suits different wave climates and depths.
learn.c2_text: Wave energy is converted through mechanical or hydraulic systems. When waves push a buoy, it drives a generator via a linear motor or hydraulic ram. Some devices store energy in pressurized fluid before converting it to electricity. This process mirrors how wind turns a turbine—but underwater motion is denser and more powerful than air.
learn.c3_text: India has launched pilot projects for ocean energy along its 7,500 km coastline. The National Institute of Ocean Technology is testing a 150 kW wave energy converter off Visakhapatnam. With plans to add 10 GW of ocean energy by 2030, India sees marine sources as a frontier in its renewable expansion strategy.

learn.title: Renewable Purchase Obligation in India Explained
learn.intro: India’s Renewable Purchase Obligation (RPO) requires utilities to source a portion of their electricity from renewable sources. It’s a key policy tool to drive demand for clean energy and meet national targets. RPOs ensure that as India expands its grid, renewables remain a core part of the energy mix.
learn.c1_text: An RPO mandates that distribution companies (DISCOMs) buy a minimum percentage of power from renewables. Currently, the central target is 175 billion units annually by 2022, increasing further. Think of it like a school requiring students to read a certain number of books—it ensures consistent engagement with the subject, here, clean energy.
learn.c2_text: Many DISCOMs struggle to meet RPOs due to financial stress and infrastructure gaps. Non-compliance leads to penalties or buying expensive renewable energy certificates (RECs). However, some states like Gujarat and Karnataka exceed targets by integrating solar parks and wind farms efficiently, showing that strong planning can overcome barriers.
learn.c3_text: Karnataka leads with over 14 GW of renewable capacity, driven by aggressive solar park development. Telangana and Andhra Pradesh also rank high. The Ministry of New and Renewable Energy tracks state-wise RPO fulfillment. In 2023, India added 18 GW of renewable capacity, helping push total installed renewables past 175 GW.

learn.title: Electric Vehicles: Motors, Braking, and Charging
learn.intro: Electric vehicles (EVs) are revolutionizing transportation by replacing internal combustion engines with efficient electric motors. They produce zero tailpipe emissions and offer instant torque, smoother rides, and lower operating costs. Understanding how EVs work—from regenerative braking to charging—is crucial for embracing sustainable mobility.
learn.c1_text: An EV uses an electric motor powered by a lithium-ion battery pack. Unlike gas engines, electric motors deliver maximum torque instantly—like a sprinter exploding from the blocks. Most EVs use AC induction or permanent magnet synchronous motors. The motor is controlled by an inverter that converts DC from the battery to AC for the wheels.
learn.c2_text: When you brake or slow down, regenerative braking captures kinetic energy and sends it back to the battery. It works like a dynamo on a bicycle—pedaling powers lights. In EVs, this system can recover up to 70% of energy normally lost as heat in traditional brakes, extending range and reducing wear on brake pads.
learn.c3_text: India aims to make 30% of new vehicle sales electric by 2030 under the FAME scheme. Over 1.1 million EVs were sold in FY2023. The government offers subsidies and is building charging infrastructure. Tata Motors and Mahindra & Mahindra lead domestic EV manufacturing, supported by policies promoting localization and affordability.

learn.title: India’s National Green Hydrogen Mission
learn.intro: India’s National Green Hydrogen Mission aims to position the country as a global leader in green hydrogen production and export. By 2030, India plans to produce 5 MMT of green hydrogen annually. This clean fuel can decarbonize hard-to-abate sectors like steel, shipping, and agriculture, supporting India’s net-zero by 2070 commitment.
learn.c1_text: Green hydrogen is made by splitting water using renewable electricity—a process called electrolysis. Unlike gray hydrogen (from fossil fuels), green hydrogen emits no CO₂. Imagine solar panels powering a machine that turns seawater into fuel. This clean molecule can store excess renewable energy and be used across industries where direct electrification isn't feasible.
learn.c2_text: Green hydrogen can replace coal in steelmaking, feed ammonia plants for fertilizers, and power fuel cells in heavy transport. For example, in steel production, hydrogen removes oxygen from iron ore instead of carbon, eliminating CO₂ emissions. It can also blend into natural gas pipelines or serve as backup power in remote areas.
learn.c3_text: Launched in 2023, the mission allocates ₹19,700 crore (~$2.3 billion) to boost green hydrogen manufacturing and exports. India plans 5 MMT annual production by 2030 and aims to become a top-3 exporter. Pilot projects are underway in Rajasthan and Tamil Nadu, leveraging cheap solar and wind to produce low-cost hydrogen.
